ch00.anchor: a keynote address to the mobilization meeting for the study of Party history
ch00.note: Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party and China’s paramount leader, launched a nationwide “Party history study and education” campaign in early 2021, the year of the Party’s centenary. He frames the whole book with this speech; the celebratory, embattled register of the pages that follow belongs to that political moment as much as to the story.—Trans.

In 2009, for the sixtieth anniversary of the People’s Republic, a national poll chose one hundred “heroes and models who made outstanding contributions to the founding of New China” and one hundred “figures who moved China” in the years since 1949; the two lists together were called the “Double Hundred.”

Not the Tang poet of the same name. Li Bai (1910–1949) was a Communist wireless operator in Shanghai, arrested and, days before the city fell to the Communists in 1949, executed by the Nationalists. His story was the basis for the celebrated 1958 film The Unfailing Radio Waves and the later ballet of the same name.

ch00.anchor: the roll of the "Three Heroes of Longtan"
ch00.note: The “Three Heroes of Longtan” (Longtan means “Dragon Pool”) were Qian Zhuangfei, Li Kenong, and Hu Di, the three Communists who penetrated the Nationalists’ own intelligence apparatus. In April 1931 their warning saved the Party’s Shanghai leadership after Gu Shunzhang defected; their story is told in Chapter Eight.

ch00.anchor: His Real Work Was to Lurk
ch00.note: The verb renders 潜伏, “to lie hidden,” to go undercover, which is also the title of Lurk (2008–2009), a hugely popular Chinese television drama about a Communist mole inside Nationalist intelligence. The pun sets the actor-grandfather’s screen roles against his real underground work.

Qian Jiang (1918–1994), Qian Zhuangfei’s son, was one of the People’s Republic’s most celebrated cinematographers; the films named here—Daughters of China, The White-Haired Girl, New Year Sacrifice, The Lin Family Shop, and Hai Xia—are classics of Chinese cinema. His documentary reportage Seven Top-Secret Telegrams lay behind the 1985 film A Nanjing Night.

A sensationalized 1996 account of Communist intelligence work, which the author holds up as the opposite of his own method; the passages he quotes turn the defector Gu Shunzhang into a lurid pulp hero.—Trans.

Gu Shunzhang, the Central Special Branch’s chief of operations, was the Party’s most damaging defector; his surrender to the Nationalists in April 1931 nearly destroyed the underground leadership (see Chapters Six through Eight). The real episode the author invokes—Gu escorting senior cadres to the Hubei-Henan-Anhui (E-Yu-Wan) base area, one of the largest Communist rural soviets—is, he complains, rewritten here as pulp fiction.
An earlier book by the author, Minguo Yi’an (2008), on unsolved criminal and political cases of the Republican period (1912–1949).

ch00.anchor: History is not a little girl to be dressed up as one pleases.
ch00.note: An inversion of a famous line—“history is a little girl anyone can dress up as they please”—popularly attributed to the scholar Hu Shi, though he never wrote it in that form. In Chinese arguments over “historical nihilism” the saying stands for the cynical view that the past can be made to mean anything; the author turns it on its head.

ch00.anchor: riches and honor cannot corrupt, poverty and low station cannot move, force and arms cannot bend
ch00.note: From the Mencius (3rd century BCE), the classic Chinese definition of the great man: one whom “riches and honor cannot corrupt, poverty and low station cannot move, force and arms cannot bend.”

ch00.anchor: the five martyrs of the League of Left-Wing Writers
ch00.note: Five young left-wing writers—Rou Shi, Yin Fu, Hu Yepin, Feng Keng, and Li Weisen—arrested and secretly shot by the Nationalists at Longhua, on the edge of Shanghai, on February 7, 1931. Lu Xun was close to several of them.
Lu Xun’s essay Wei le wangque de jinian (1933), written to mourn the five and to defy the silence around them; the closing lines paraphrased here are among the most quoted in modern Chinese prose.

ch00.anchor: oppose historical nihilism under a clear banner
ch00.note: “Historical nihilism” (lishi xuwu zhuyi) is an official term in the People’s Republic for accounts that question the received, celebratory version of Party history; combating it has been a stated aim of state cultural policy under Xi Jinping. The author writes squarely from within that campaign.—Trans.

ch00.anchor: the Sixth National Security Education Day for All
ch00.note: April 15 was designated China’s annual National Security Education Day under the 2015 National Security Law; 2021 was the sixth. The date of the author’s signature is itself a statement of the book’s theme.—Trans.
